questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Natural Logarithm Function Using the Chain Rule
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $g(x)$ as the composite function

$$
g=ln⁡u,\,u={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{u}\cdot 2x \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\cdot 2x \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2\cancel{x}}{x\cdot \cancel{x}} \\  & =\frac{2}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a General Logarithm Function Using the Chain Rule
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=log⁡u={log}_{10}⁡(u),\,u=1-x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{uln⁡(10)},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-1.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{uln⁡(10)}\cdot (-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{(1-x)ln⁡(10)}\cdot (-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{(1-x)ln⁡(10)}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $f(x)=ln⁡(2-x)$ at the point $(1,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f=ln⁡u,\,u=2-x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-1.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{u}\cdot (-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2-x}\cdot (-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{x-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope $m$ of the tangent line at the point where $x=1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={\frac{1}{x-2}|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(1)-2} \\  & =-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the slope of the tangent line at the point $(1,0)$ is $m=-1.$ Now, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-0 & =(-1)\cdot (x-1) \\ y & =-x+1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a General Logarithm Function Using the Chain Rule
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=log⁡(u),\,u={x}^{5}-2.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{uln⁡(10)},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5{x}^{4}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{uln⁡(10)}\cdot 5{x}^{4} \\  & =\frac{5{x}^{4}}{({x}^{5}-2)ln⁡(10)}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a General Logarithm Function Using the Chain Rule
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={log}_{4}⁡(u),\,u=\sqrt{7x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{uln⁡(4)},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{7}{2\sqrt{7x}}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{uln⁡(4)}\cdot \frac{7}{2\sqrt{7x}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{7x}ln⁡(4)}\cdot \frac{7}{2\sqrt{7x}} \\  & =\frac{7}{2\cdot 7xln⁡(4)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{7}}{2\cdot \cancel{7}xln⁡(4)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2xln⁡(4)}.\end{aligned}
$$
